questions.q: What problem does the "one trigger per object" pattern specifically solve?
options: It eliminates the need for governor limits entirely on that object
It allows the object to bypass validation rules

Unpredictable execution order and multiplied governor limit cost from multiple independent triggers on the same object, by consolidating all logic into a single trigger that delegates to a handler class
It automatically converts synchronous triggers into asynchronous ones
questions.explain: Multiple independent triggers on the same object have no guaranteed order and each may duplicate queries or DML, multiplying the real cost of a single transaction — one trigger delegating to a handler class consolidates and controls that.

questions.q: In the recursion example, why does update toUpdate; inside an after-update trigger risk infinite or wasteful recursion?
options: Because update statements are not allowed inside after-update triggers at all
Because that DML statement fires the same object's after-update trigger again, which can reprocess records that were already handled in the same transaction
Because it exceeds the DML row limit on the very first execution
Because recursion only happens in before-triggers, never in after-triggers
questions.explain: Any DML on the same object inside its own trigger re-invokes that trigger, so without a guard, logic that updates a field and saves can keep re-triggering itself on the records it just changed.

questions.q: Why is a static variable the right scope for a recursion guard?
options: Because static variables persist for the life of a single transaction but reset automatically on the next separate transaction, which matches exactly the scope needed to prevent re-entry within one transaction
Because static variables persist permanently across all future transactions in the org
Because static variables are the only way to declare a Boolean in Apex
Because static variables automatically disable governor limits when set to true
questions.explain: A recursion guard needs to block re-entry only within the current transaction, and reset for the next one — exactly how a static variable behaves in Apex's execution context.

questions.q: Why can a poorly-built Flow cause the exact same kind of governor limit problem as a non-bulkified trigger?
options: Because Flow automation is actually executed as hidden Apex code behind the scenes with its own separate limits
Because Flows are exempt from governor limits, so this is never actually a real risk
Because Flow can only process one record at a time, unlike Apex triggers

Because Flow runs inside the same transaction and against the same governor limits as Apex, so a Get Records or DML element placed inside a Flow loop consumes limit budget per iteration, just like SOQL or DML inside an Apex loop
questions.explain: Flow shares the same transaction and governor limit budget as Apex. A Get/Create/Update Records element inside a loop is the declarative equivalent of SOQL or DML inside an Apex loop, with the same per-record cost multiplication.

questions.q: Why might a governor limit exception that appears to come from a trigger actually be caused by a Flow instead?
options: Because Flows always run after every trigger has already thrown its own separate exception
Because Salesforce mislabels all Flow errors as Apex trigger errors by default

Because Flow and Apex share the same transaction boundary (per Lesson 5), so a Flow consuming limit budget inefficiently can be the real cause even though the exception's stack trace points at a trigger running later in the same transaction
This can never happen; Flow errors are always reported separately from Apex errors
questions.explain: Because Flow and Apex share one transaction and one cumulative governor limit budget, a Flow that wastefully consumes that budget earlier in the transaction can be the real root cause of an exception that surfaces later, in a trigger that looks unrelated.
